pages.summary: An array padded on its sides.
body: By padsize along each dimension: with a value (0), or by repeating the array (`'circular'`), its border (`'replicate'`) or its mirror image (`'symmetric'`); on both sides (the default), or only before or after.
syntax: A value or a method, on a side.

pages.summary: An image worked on block by block, or neighbourhood by neighbourhood.
body: `im2col` makes each m-by-n block a column (every position, `'sliding'`, or tiles, `'distinct'`), and `col2im` puts columns back. `blockproc` calls a function on each m-by-n block (with a struct of its data, location and size) and puts the results together in the blocks' places, with a border of neighbours if asked. `nlfilter` calls a function on every pixel's neighbourhood, giving the pixel's value; `colfilt` gives the function all the blocks at once as columns, which is much faster for functions that work on columns.

examples.title: Block means two ways
A local maximum two ways

pages.summary: One level of an image pyramid: half the size, or twice.
body: `'reduce'` smooths by Burt and Adelson's 5-tap kernel and keeps every other pixel (ceil(M/2) rows); `'expand'` makes it twice as large less one, interpolating. A pyramid of reductions looks at an image at several scales.

examples.title: Three levels down and one back up

pages.summary: Values along a path through an image, and an image's contour lines.
body: `improfile` samples the image along the path through the points (xi, yi), at n evenly spaced points (about one per pixel of the path's length unless given), `'nearest'` unless `'bilinear'` or `'bicubic'`; NaN off the image. Without outputs it plots the profile. `imcontour` draws contour lines in the image's orientation (rows down, square pixels).
syntax: c = improfile(I, xi, yi, n, method)

examples.title: Across the phantom, and its contours

pages.summary: Straight lines found by the Hough transform.
body: `hough` lets each on pixel of a binary image vote for every line through it: at each angle theta (-90 to 89 degrees), the distance rho = x cos(theta) + y sin(theta) from the origin (x and y from 0). `houghpeaks` finds the largest votes, clearing each one's neighbourhood before looking for the next; `houghlines` follows the pixels along each peak's line and gives the segments, joining gaps up to `'FillGap'` and keeping those at least `'MinLength'` long.
syntax: lines = houghlines(BW, theta, rho, peaks, 'FillGap', g, 'MinLength', m)

examples.title: Two lines in a field of specks

pages.summary: Circles found by a circular Hough transform.
body: Each strong edge pixel (its Sobel gradient above a threshold, Otsu's by default) votes along its gradient for centres at the radii in a range, towards the brighter side (`'ObjectPolarity'` `'bright'`) or the darker; at each peak the radius is the commonest distance of the pixels that voted, and the metric the share of the circle lying on an edge. Circles with a metric of at least 1 - `'Sensitivity'` (0.85) are kept, the strongest first.
syntax: [centers, radii, metric] = imfindcircles(A, [rmin rmax], 'ObjectPolarity', p, 'Sensitivity', s)

examples.title: Three coins

pages.summary: The Radon transform, its inverse by filtered back projection, and the phantom to test them on.
body: `radon` integrates the image along lines at each angle (counterclockwise from the x axis, 0:179), giving one projection per column, at distances xp from the centre; this is what a CT scanner measures. `iradon` reconstructs the image by filtering each projection (`'Ram-Lak'` by default, or smoother filters) and spreading it back. `phantom` gives the Shepp-Logan head phantom, ellipses of known intensities (the modified one, with more contrast, by default), or ellipses of one's own.
syntax: I = iradon(R, theta, interp, filter, frequency_scaling, output_size)
Of a type, with its ellipses.

examples.title: Projected and reconstructed

pages.summary: The two-dimensional discrete cosine transform, its inverse, and its matrix.
body: `dct2` gives the orthonormal 2-D DCT of type II (the image padded or cut to m-by-n first): a smooth image's energy gathers in the coefficients near the top left corner, the basis of JPEG compression. `idct2` inverts it; `dctmtx` gives the n-by-n matrix D with `D*A*D'` equal to `dct2(A)`.
